newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Alarm grows in Italy over EMU prospects.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Alarm grows in Italy over EMU prospects.

text.p: The Italian Treasury is seeking to bolster its 1997 budget amid fears that EU partners will not relax the criteria for founder members of the planned single European currency, economic commentators said on Tuesday.

The budget is due to be unveiled at the end of the week and Prime Minister Romano Prodi has undertaken an unexpected last minute round of negotiations with supporters of his centre-left government to try to give the package more bite.
"There has been a much greater awareness over the past three weeks of the risks of being left out economic and monetary union (EMU)," a senior government source said.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi has said the budget will seek to cut 32.4 trillion lire ($21.2 billion) off next year's deficit, but this total might have to be increased to cover a growing hole in 1996 accounts.

Newspapers said on Tuesday the package may be raised to 40 trillion lire, but even this would not cut Italy's 1997 deficit to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio to the required three percent level as called for by the Maastricht Treaty.
Current government forecasts predict Italy's deficit/GDP ratio will be 4.52 percent next year and 2.99 percent in 1998.
The government had hoped that signs it was moving towards the three percent threshold would be enough to secure a berth at the launch of EMU in 1999.

That hope is now fading. The alarm bells really began ringing when Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar told Prodi last week that Spain would do all in its power to meet the strict Maastricht terms and enter EMU from the start.

The worries increased at a weekend meeting of EU finance ministers and central bank governors in Ireland when the European Commission revealed in a document obtained by Reuters that it expected there to be just seven founder EMU countries.
A commission official indicated that Italy would not make the grade without tough additional budget adjustments.
The idea of being left isolated on the southern fringes of Europe along with Greece has sent a shiver through the government, which fears that there might only be one chance to join EMU.

"There can no longer be a situation where some arrive first and others later, but there will be a large number of countries that enter right away," Prodi told reporters during a trip in the Netherlands.
"Not being among these countries means economic ruin for Italy," he said in comments broadcast by Italian television.
Any sign that Italy was losing sight of its EMU goal would also hit market sentiment.
In a bid to strenghten Italy's hand, Ciampi wants to tackle sensitive spending areas such as pensions and health. This is taboo territory for the hard-left Communist Refoundation.
Although the party is not formally a part of the government coalition, Prodi relies on its votes to secure a majority in the lower house of parliament.

However, Refoundation has said it might support a special "Maastricht Tax" to raise swift revenues for the debt-laden government. Analysts say such a "solidarity tax" might produce much more money than cuts to pensions and health.

"The only way for Italy to get a convincing budget at this late stage is to go for a special tax for monetary union," Lorenzo Codogno, analyst at Bank of America in Milan, told Reuters Financial Television.
